title: How do telecom companies make money, and what matters in a telecom case?
description: Telecom economics for case interviews: ARPU, churn, network investment, subscriber acquisition cost and price competition, with a worked churn example.
hook: Mobile and broadband companies spend enormous sums on networks, then compete hard for customers who can switch fairly easily. That combination makes churn and price competition the heart of most telecom cases.
body:
How telecoms make money

Monthly plans for mobile, broadband and TV, plus handset sales and business services. Revenue = subscribers × ARPU (average revenue per user).

Heavy fixed investment

Networks, spectrum licences and fibre are huge upfront costs. Once built, an extra customer costs little to serve, so filling the network matters (high operating leverage).

A worked example: the cost of churn

An operator has 10M subscribers paying £20 a month. Monthly churn rises from 1.5% to 2%: an extra 50,000 customers leave each month. Over a year that is 600,000 extra departures, roughly £144M of lost yearly revenue if not replaced (600,000 × £20 × 12), before counting the cost of winning replacements.

The levers

  • Retention offers at contract end.
  • Bundles (mobile plus broadband) that raise switching costs.
  • Network quality, which drives satisfaction.
  • Price tiers that protect ARPU.

Typical telecom case questions

  • Why is churn rising, and how do we reduce it?
  • Should we respond to a rival's price cut?
  • Should we invest in fibre in rural areas?

Measure the economics of losing one subscriber

A mobile operator has 2 million subscribers, average monthly revenue per user (ARPU) of £20 and monthly churn of 1.5%. It loses about 30,000 subscribers per month before new additions. Cutting churn to 1.2% would reduce gross losses to 24,000, retaining around 6,000 additional subscribers in the first month. At £20 ARPU that cohort represents £120,000 of monthly revenue before network and service costs, but the benefit accumulates differently over time as retained customers may later churn.

A first-year estimate that multiplies 6,000 by twelve months would overstate recurring incremental customers if you assume the same cohort is retained forever. Instead build a simple monthly subscriber bridge: closing base = opening base + gross additions − disconnections. Repeat it across periods, and calculate revenue using the relevant average active subscriber base. This also helps reveal whether a marketing campaign is improving growth or merely replacing lost customers.

The strategic constraint is the network: spectrum, towers and fibre often require large upfront investment. Filling spare capacity can be profitable, but aggressive discounts may teach customers to expect lower prices and increase price-driven churn later. Segment prepaid, contract, family plans and enterprise customers because ARPU, acquisition cost and retention vary.

A strong next question is whether the churn increase is concentrated in a region, tariff or tenure cohort. That helps distinguish poor service quality from a competitor's targeted offer.
